title: Pistol shrimp fire collapsing bubbles that can stun prey.
hook: One tiny claw creates a shock wave, a flash of light and the crackle of an entire reef.

image.alt: Orange-and-white tiger snapping shrimp, Alpheus bellulus, partly sheltered in a reef crevice.
image.credit: Dan Schofield · CC BY 4.0 · may be cropped and darkened by website display

levels.title: The claw is a water pistol, not a pair of castanets.

objects.title: A moving plunger squeezes water through a nozzle
objects.text: In species such as Alpheus heterochaelis, the oversized claw has a protruding plunger and a matching socket. When the movable half shuts, it forces water out through a narrow channel. Researchers measured a jet around 25 metres per second: the fast-moving water, not the two claw surfaces striking, sets up the weapon.

sources.title: How snapping shrimp snap: through cavitating bubbles
A unique way of sound production in the snapping shrimp (Alpheus heterochaelis)
sources.publisher: Schmitz et al. · Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2000

levels.title: The 'bullet' is a pocket of water vapour.

objects.title: Try the cavitation lab
objects.description: Change the controls to explore bubble formation and collapse in a simplified model. Compare the results with the measured mechanism.

objects.title: Fast flow makes liquid water turn into vapour
objects.text: As the jet rushes outward, it curls into a spinning vortex. Pressure can plunge inside that swirl; when it falls sufficiently low, local water vaporizes and leaves a cavity. This is cavitation, not a bubble of air blown out of the claw. Normal surrounding pressure then works to crush it.

sources.title: Vortex Formation with a Snapping Shrimp Claw
Unveiling the physical mechanism behind pistol shrimp cavitation

objects.title: Scientists rebuilt the flow at a larger scale
objects.text: A 2013 experiment used an enlarged mechanical plunger-and-socket claw and photographed the flow. It produced a leading vortex ring, a rotating doughnut of water. Later computer simulations predicted that sufficiently strong swirl creates the low-pressure, cavitating ring. The enlarged model demonstrated the vortex, not a full live-shrimp attack.

sources.title: Vortex Formation with a Snapping Shrimp Claw
Unveiling the physical mechanism behind pistol shrimp cavitation

levels.title: The real snap happens after the claw closes.

objects.title: High-speed cameras overturned the obvious explanation
objects.text: In 2000, researchers filmed the claw at 40,500 frames per second while recording sound with an underwater microphone called a hydrophone. The sharp sound occurred when the bubble collapsed, after the claw had already shut. The bubble implosion, not the mechanical click, was responsible for the acoustic blast.

sources.title: How snapping shrimp snap: through cavitating bubbles
On the sound of snapping shrimp
sources.publisher: Versluis et al. · University of Twente, 2001

objects.title: The collapsing cavity pushes a pressure pulse through water
objects.text: When the vapour cavity contracts violently, water rushes inward and a brief, intense pressure wave spreads outward. Snapping shrimp use this close-range effect to stun or kill small prey and to defend themselves. Calling it a 'bubble bullet' is vivid, but it is the pressure pulse that does the striking.

sources.title: How snapping shrimp snap: through cavitating bubbles
Bioinspired mechanical device generates plasma in water via cavitation

levels.title: The same bubble briefly flashes with light.

objects.title: Sensitive detectors caught the nearly invisible flash
objects.text: In 2001, Lohse, Schmitz and Versluis detected light at the instant snapping-shrimp bubbles collapsed. They named it shrimpoluminescence, a biological example resembling sonoluminescence. The researchers inferred temperatures of at least 5,000 kelvin inside the collapsing bubble. That fleeting, microscopic hot spot is not the same thing as heating nearby seawater or cooking prey.

sources.title: Snapping shrimp make flashing bubbles

objects.title: Single-bubble sonoluminescence
objects.publisher: Brenner, Hilgenfeldt & Lohse · Reviews of Modern Physics, 2002
objects.description: In laboratory sonoluminescence, an ultrasound-driven bubble focuses energy as it collapses. Models favour extreme heating and partial ionization of gas, causing a tiny flash; the precise microscopic emission mechanism is more complex than a bubble simply glowing like a light bulb.

objects.title: They scanned a shed claw and built a spring-loaded replica
objects.text: In 2019, engineers scanned the three-dimensional shape of a striped snapping shrimp's shed claw, printed a version five times larger and drove it underwater with springs. They captured cavitation, shock waves and light emission. The light supported their interpretation of plasma formation during collapse; the imitation was a laboratory device, not a robot hunting prey.

sources.title: Bioinspired mechanical device generates plasma in water via cavitation

objects.title: See the original lab measurements and images
objects.description: Figure 3 combines fast-camera frames, bubble-size measurements and schlieren images of the expanding pressure front. Light emission from the device was extremely faint and the experiment used gas-doped water to make its detection easier.

levels.title: Baby snapping shrimp have astonishing acceleration.

objects.title: A millimetre-scale claw moves with extraordinary acceleration
objects.text: Harrison and Patek filmed juvenile bigclaw snapping shrimp at 300,000 frames per second. Their 2023 study measured mean peak accelerations of about 580,000 metres per second squared, with substantial variation: a record in the study for reusable underwater movements. Even tiny juveniles could generate cavitation; acceleration is not the same as top speed.

sources.title: Developing elastic mechanisms: ultrafast motion and cavitation emerge at the millimeter scale in juvenile snapping shrimp
sources.publisher: Harrison & Patek · Journal of Experimental Biology, 2023

objects.title: Watch the original 300,000-fps juvenile recording
objects.publisher: Journal of Experimental Biology · research movie, 2023
objects.description: The journal's research movie shows a juvenile snap filmed at 300,000 frames per second and played at 30 frames per second. This is laboratory footage of the tiny claw, slowed dramatically so a human can see the motion.

levels.title: Lose the big claw and the other one can become the gun.

objects.title: The small pincer transforms into a snapper
objects.text: Many Alpheus snapping shrimp have one large firing claw and one small grasping pincer. Experiments removing the large claw showed a remarkable reversal: the remaining small claw transforms into a new large snapper while a replacement small pincer regrows at the lost claw's site. The exact schedule depends on growth and moulting.

sources.title: Remodeling of nerves during claw reversal in adult snapping shrimps
sources.publisher: Govind & Pearce · Journal of Comparative Neurology, 1988

sources.title: Post-autotomy claw regrowth and functional recovery in the snapping shrimp Alpheus angulosus
sources.publisher: Marine and Freshwater Behaviour and Physiology, 2014

objects.title: The nervous system starts changing before the claw is rebuilt
objects.text: A 1988 study found that, after claw loss, nerves serving the surviving little pincer began shifting toward the large-claw pattern within days. This neural remodeling preceded the more visible changes in muscle and shell. The animal is not merely growing a new tool; it is reconfiguring how that tool is controlled.

sources.title: Remodeling of nerves during claw reversal in adult snapping shrimps
sources.publisher: Govind & Pearce · Journal of Comparative Neurology, 1988

levels.title: Some armed shrimp recruit a lookout fish.

objects.title: One partner digs; the other watches for danger
objects.text: In several shrimp-goby partnerships, the shrimp excavates and maintains a shelter while a goby stays near its entrance. When danger approaches, the fish can give tactile warning signals and both retreat into the burrow. The shrimp's poor vision makes the fish's vigilance especially valuable; not every snapping-shrimp species has this relationship.

sources.title: Behavioural interdependence in a shrimp–goby mutualism
sources.publisher: Burns et al. · Journal of Zoology, 2019

sources.title: Species-specific behaviors drive the initiation and maintenance of snapping shrimp-goby mutualisms

objects.title: A goby and its snapping-shrimp partner

image.alt: A spotted goby, Amblyeleotris yanoi, hovering over an orange-and-white Alpheus randalli snapping shrimp beside a sandy burrow.
image.credit: Steve Childs · CC BY 2.0 · photo may be cropped and darkened by website display

objects.caption: A photographed Amblyeleotris yanoi and Alpheus randalli pair. This image shows the partners together, not the instant a danger signal is sent.

objects.title: How the fish and shrimp start living together
objects.description: In filmed encounters between tiger shrimp and yellow watchman gobies, gobies usually initiated contact. Shrimp dug shelter, and established shrimp spent more time contacting their familiar goby than an unfamiliar one.

levels.title: Other shrimp snap together like an armed colony.

objects.title: Some sponge-dwelling shrimp live in queen-and-defender societies
objects.text: Certain Synalpheus snapping shrimp inhabit marine sponges in related groups with one or a few breeding females and many nonbreeding defenders. This form of eusociality, familiar from ants and bees, is extraordinary among marine animals. It is a different shrimp lineage and social arrangement from the goby-sharing Alpheus species.

sources.title: Social transitions in sponge-dwelling snapping shrimp
sources.publisher: Chak et al. · Current Opinion in Insect Science, 2019

sources.title: Colony Structure of the Social Snapping Shrimp Synalpheus Filidigitus in Belize

objects.title: One defender triggers a chorus of warning snaps
objects.text: In a 2006 experiment, a sentinel's reaction to an intruding shrimp recruited other colony members to snap in concert for seconds or longer. The defenders did not swarm toward the enemy; the coordinated sound appeared to advertise that a well-defended sponge was occupied. Their claws functioned as communication devices as well as weapons.

sources.title: Coordinated group response to nest intruders in social shrimp

levels.title: A shrimp-made crackle can help young corals find home.

objects.title: Thousands of little snaps become an underwater soundscape
objects.text: A hydrophone over a shallow reef hears a steady crackle rather than isolated pistol shots. Shrimp snaps can dominate the higher-frequency part of reef recordings, alongside fish calls and other sounds. The noise can be useful information about habitat, although its loudness alone is not a complete measure of reef health.

sources.title: The Curious Acoustic Behavior of Estuarine Snapping Shrimp: Temporal Patterns of Snapping Shrimp Sound in Sub-Tidal Oyster Reef Habitat
The utility of different acoustic indicators to describe biological sounds of a coral reef soundscape

objects.title: Playing healthy-reef sound increased coral-larva settlement
objects.publisher: Aoki et al. · Royal Society Open Science, 2024
objects.description: At a degraded reef, researchers played soundscapes recorded from healthy reefs. Larvae of the coral Porites astreoides settled about 1.7 times as often at acoustically enriched sites on average. The recordings included shrimp and fish, so the experiment does not isolate shrimp snaps as the sole cause.
